dinosaur_day.label: Dinosaur Day
dinosaur_day.intro: A day for the giants that ruled the planet long before us. Museums, model kits and children who can pronounce Parasaurolophus faster than any adult all get their moment.
funFacts: Richard Owen coined the word dinosaur in 1842 from Greek roots meaning roughly terrible or fearfully great lizard.
Birds are living dinosaurs: they descend from small feathered theropods, so a sparrow is closer kin to T. rex than any lizard.
More time separates Stegosaurus from Tyrannosaurus rex than separates T. rex from us.

rocky_road_day.label: National Rocky Road Day
rocky_road_day.intro: Chocolate ice cream with marshmallows and nuts in it: rocky road is the flavour that refuses to be smooth. A day to order the scoop with the most texture.
funFacts: Ice cream maker William Dreyer is credited with the flavour in 1929, reportedly cutting marshmallows with his wife's sewing scissors.
In Australia and Britain rocky road is not ice cream at all but a chilled chocolate bar full of marshmallow and nuts.
Marshmallows once really did contain marsh mallow: the root sap of Althaea officinalis was whipped with sugar.

world_bicycle_day.label: World Bicycle Day
world_bicycle_day.intro: Two wheels, no fuel, and the same basic shape for over a century. This day celebrates the most efficient machine ever built for moving a human being.
funFacts: The UN General Assembly declared 3 June World Bicycle Day in April 2018.
Karl Drais rode his Laufmaschine near Mannheim in 1817, the pedal-free ancestor of every bicycle since.
The Netherlands has more bicycles than people, with well over 20 million bikes for around 18 million inhabitants.

cheese_day.label: National Cheese Day
cheese_day.intro: Fresh, blue, hard, runny or grilled: cheese is milk that learned to keep. A day to build a cheese board and eat the crumbs off the paper.
funFacts: It takes roughly ten litres of milk to make one kilogram of hard cheese.
The holes in Emmental are gas bubbles: propionic acid bacteria give off carbon dioxide as the wheel ripens.
Traces of cheese-making were found on 7,000-year-old pottery sieves from Poland, some of the oldest evidence known.

gingerbread_day.label: National Gingerbread Day
gingerbread_day.intro: Gingerbread is not just for December. This day puts the spiced dough back on the table in the middle of summer, whether as a soft cookie or a crisp little house.
funFacts: Nuremberg has been famous for Lebkuchen since the Middle Ages, helped by its position on the spice trade routes.
Gingerbread men are traditionally credited to the court of Elizabeth I, who had them baked in the likeness of guests.
The heat in ginger comes from gingerol, a chemical relative of the compounds that make chilli and pepper sharp.

yo_yo_day.label: National Yo-Yo Day
yo_yo_day.intro: A disc, an axle and a string. The yo-yo has been going up and down for over two thousand years and still turns up in every school playground.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Donald F. Duncan, the businessman who turned the yo-yo into an American craze in the 1930s.
A Greek vase from around 440 BC shows a boy playing with a disc toy that looks remarkably like a yo-yo.
In 1985 a yo-yo flew aboard Space Shuttle Discovery so astronauts could film how it behaves without gravity.

chocolate_ice_cream_day.label: National Chocolate Ice Cream Day
chocolate_ice_cream_day.intro: Vanilla may be the bestseller, but chocolate came first. A day for the darkest scoop in the freezer, in a cone, a cup or straight from the tub.
funFacts: A Neapolitan recipe collection from 1692 already described frozen chocolate, decades before vanilla ice cream was written down.
Cocoa pods grow straight out of the trunk of the cacao tree, a growth habit botanists call cauliflory.
Good ice cream is mostly about small ice crystals, which is why the mixture has to be churned while it freezes.

best_friends_day.label: National Best Friends Day
best_friends_day.intro: The person who knows your worst stories and stays anyway. This day is a nudge to actually call them instead of just thinking about it.
funFacts: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar suggests we manage around 150 stable relationships, but only about five truly close ones.
Merriam-Webster added the abbreviation BFF to its dictionary in 2010, decades after teenagers invented it.
Knotted friendship bracelets come from Central and South American macramé traditions and spread worldwide in the 1980s.

donald_duck_day.label: National Donald Duck Day
donald_duck_day.intro: Sailor shirt, no trousers, and a temper that never lasts long. This day marks the screen debut of the most famous duck in the world.
funFacts: Donald first appeared on 9 June 1934 in the Silly Symphony short The Wise Little Hen.
Clarence Nash created the squawking voice and kept performing it for around fifty years.
German readers know him through Erika Fuchs, whose witty translations put words like seufz and ächz into everyday language.

world_art_nouveau_day.label: World Art Nouveau Day
world_art_nouveau_day.intro: Curving iron, whiplash lines and flowers growing across facades: a day for the style that briefly turned whole cities into ornament, from Barcelona to Brussels to Riga.
funFacts: The date marks the death day of two masters of the style, Antoni Gaudí and the Hungarian architect Ödön Lechner.
The same movement has a different name almost everywhere: Jugendstil in Germany, Modernisme in Catalonia, Secession in Vienna.
Hector Guimard's cast-iron Paris Métro entrances from around 1900 are among the most photographed pieces of the style.

international_lynx_day.label: International Lynx Day
international_lynx_day.intro: Tufted ears, enormous paws and a talent for staying invisible: a day for the shy cat that quietly returned to Europe's forests.
funFacts: The Eurasian lynx is the largest wild cat in Europe, with males reaching well over 20 kilograms.
Its wide, furry paws work like snowshoes and let it cross deep snow that would swallow other predators.
Hunted out in Germany during the 19th century, the lynx was reintroduced to the Harz mountains from 2000 onwards.

red_rose_day.label: National Red Rose Day
red_rose_day.intro: One flower says more than most sentences. This day belongs to the red rose, in the garden, on the table or handed over without much explanation.
funFacts: Roses have been cultivated for around 5,000 years, and fossil roses are some 35 million years old.
It takes several tonnes of petals to distil a single kilogram of rose oil, which is why the essence costs more than gold by weight.
The Victorian language of flowers pinned each colour to a message, and red was reserved for declared love.

sewing_machine_day.label: National Sewing Machine Day
sewing_machine_day.intro: The machine that took clothing out of the hand-stitched era. A day for the quiet workhorse in the cupboard and everyone who still repairs instead of replaces.
funFacts: Elias Howe patented a lockstitch machine in 1846, and Isaac Singer's marketing turned it into a household object.
Barthélemy Thimonnier's Paris sewing workshop was wrecked in 1831 by tailors who feared for their livelihoods.
A lockstitch needs two threads: the needle thread from above and the bobbin thread hidden underneath.

strawberry_shortcake_day.label: National Strawberry Shortcake Day
strawberry_shortcake_day.intro: Sweet biscuit, sliced strawberries, a cloud of whipped cream. The dessert that marks the start of proper summer, best eaten outdoors.
funFacts: Strawberries are not botanically berries: the tiny pips on the outside are the real fruits, and there are around 200 per strawberry.
The garden strawberry is a hybrid, bred in Brittany around 1750 from a Chilean and a North American species.
In the American original the shortcake is a crumbly biscuit, not the sponge base sold in Europe.

lobster_day.label: National Lobster Day
lobster_day.intro: Once so common it was fed to prisoners, now the centrepiece of the menu. A day for the armoured crustacean with the outsized claws.
funFacts: In colonial New England lobster was cheap fare for servants and inmates, and contracts limited how often it could be served.
Lobster blood is bluish because it carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.
A live lobster is mottled brown; heat frees the red pigment astaxanthin from its protein and the shell turns scarlet.

bloomsday.label: Bloomsday
bloomsday.intro: Dublin spends this day walking through a novel. Readers in Edwardian dress retrace the route of Leopold Bloom, book in hand, from breakfast to the small hours.
funFacts: The whole of James Joyce's Ulysses takes place on a single day, Thursday 16 June 1904, in Dublin.
Joyce chose the date because it was the day he first walked out with Nora Barnacle, who later became his wife.
The first Bloomsday was staged in 1954 for the fiftieth anniversary, and the pilgrims never made it to the end of the route.

apple_strudel_day.label: National Apple Strudel Day
apple_strudel_day.intro: Paper-thin pastry, apples, raisins, cinnamon and a snowfall of icing sugar. A day for the most patient piece of baking in Central European kitchens.
funFacts: The oldest known strudel recipes date from 1696 and survive in a handwritten cookbook kept in Vienna.
The dough is stretched by hand until you can supposedly read a newspaper through it.
Strudel means whirlpool in German, which is exactly what the rolled-up cross-section looks like.

sushi_day.label: International Sushi Day
sushi_day.intro: Rice, vinegar, fish and a lot of practice. Sushi travelled from Japanese street stalls to almost every city on earth, and this day toasts the journey.
funFacts: The word sushi refers to the seasoned rice, not the fish on top of it.
Its ancestor narezushi was a preservation method: fish was fermented in rice, and the rice was thrown away.
Nigiri appeared in early 19th-century Edo as fast food sold from stalls, meant to be eaten standing up with your fingers.

world_sauntering_day.label: World Sauntering Day
world_sauntering_day.intro: Not a run, not a march, not even a brisk walk. Today the correct speed is slow enough to notice things, with no destination worth hurrying towards.
funFacts: The day was dreamed up in 1979 at the Grand Hotel on Mackinac Island as a gentle protest against the jogging boom.
That hotel porch is one of the longest in the world at around 200 metres, which makes it ideal for the purpose.
A popular folk etymology derives saunter from à la Sainte Terre, the stroll of a pilgrim to the Holy Land.

vanilla_milkshake_day.label: National Vanilla Milkshake Day
vanilla_milkshake_day.intro: Milk, ice cream, vanilla, and a straw that never quite copes. The plainest milkshake on the menu is still the one most people order twice.
funFacts: In the 1880s a milkshake was an adult drink: eggs, cream and a shot of whisky, shaken by hand.
Vanilla comes from an orchid whose flowers open for a single day and are pollinated by hand almost everywhere.
The technique was worked out by Edmond Albius on Réunion in 1841, when he was still a teenager.

world_music_day.label: World Music Day
world_music_day.intro: On the longest day of the year, amateurs and professionals play for free in streets, courtyards and parks. Anyone with an instrument is allowed on stage, because there is no stage.
funFacts: The Fête de la Musique started in Paris in 1982, launched by culture minister Jack Lang and Maurice Fleuret.
The French name is a pun: fête de la musique sounds like faites de la musique, meaning make music.
It is now celebrated in around 120 countries; Berlin has held its own edition since 1995.

onion_ring_day.label: National Onion Ring Day
onion_ring_day.intro: A slice of onion, a jacket of batter, hot oil and nothing else. The side order that quietly steals attention from whatever it was ordered with.
funFacts: John Mollard's cookbook of 1802 already describes onion rings dipped in batter and fried, long before diners existed.
Onions make you cry because cutting releases an enzyme that produces the irritant syn-propanethial-S-oxide.
Chilling the onion first slows that reaction down, which is why a cold onion is a kinder onion.

olympic_day.label: Olympic Day
olympic_day.intro: A day when clubs, schools and cities put on runs and open training sessions for anyone who turns up. The Olympic idea, minus the qualifying times.
funFacts: The date marks the founding of the International Olympic Committee at the Sorbonne in Paris on 23 June 1894.
The first Olympic Day was held in 1948 in nine countries, from Portugal and Greece to Uruguay and Canada.
The Olympic Day Run followed in 1987 and is now open to anyone, whatever their pace.

international_fairy_day.label: International Fairy Day
international_fairy_day.intro: Tiny doors at the foot of trees, glitter in the garden and stories that stay deliberately unproven. A day for the small folk of European folklore.
funFacts: The Cottingley Fairies photographs of 1917 convinced Arthur Conan Doyle; the cousins admitted the cut-out hoax only in 1983.
Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream gave the fairy world its best-known cast: Titania, Oberon and Puck.
Fairy rings of mushrooms are real: a fungus spreads outwards underground and fruits along the growing edge.

global_beatles_day.label: Global Beatles Day
global_beatles_day.intro: Four musicians from Liverpool, roughly ten years of recording, and a shadow over popular music ever since. A day to play the albums loudly and in order.
funFacts: The date recalls 25 June 1967, when the band played All You Need Is Love live on the first worldwide satellite broadcast.
That programme, Our World, reached an estimated 400 to 700 million viewers, the largest television audience up to then.
The zebra crossing from the Abbey Road cover was given listed heritage status in 2010.

world_refrigeration_day.label: World Refrigeration Day
world_refrigeration_day.intro: The most underrated machine in the house. Without cooling there would be no fresh milk in June, no ice cream and no medicine that survives the journey.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Lord Kelvin, born 26 June 1824, who gave his name to the absolute temperature scale.
Before machines there was the ice trade: blocks cut from New England lakes were shipped as far as India.
Carl von Linde built a working ammonia refrigeration machine in Munich in the 1870s, and brewers were among his first customers.

sunglasses_day.label: National Sunglasses Day
sunglasses_day.intro: Half eye protection, half disguise. On the shortest nights of the year, sunglasses get their own day, whether on the nose or pushed into the hair.
funFacts: Inuit peoples carved slitted snow goggles from bone or antler long before glass lenses existed.
Chinese judges are said to have used smoke-coloured quartz lenses to keep their expressions unreadable in court.
Polarised lenses arrived in 1936, when Edwin Land applied his Polaroid filter material to sunglasses.

tau_day.label: Tau Day
tau_day.intro: A quietly rebellious day for anyone who thinks the circle constant should be 6.28, not 3.14. Tradition demands twice as much pie as on Pi Day.
funFacts: Tau is defined as two pi, roughly 6.28, which is why the date falls on 6/28.
A full turn is one tau in radians, so a quarter circle is simply tau over four instead of pi over two.
The idea gained followers through Bob Palais' 2001 article Pi Is Wrong and Michael Hartl's Tau Manifesto of 2010.

camera_day.label: National Camera Day
camera_day.intro: From a wooden box with a brass lens to the thing in your pocket. A day for photography and for the boxes of old prints nobody can throw away.
funFacts: The camera obscura was described in detail around 1020 by the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, centuries before film.
The oldest surviving photograph, Nicéphore Niépce's view from a window, needed an exposure of many hours.
Oskar Barnack's Leica of 1925 made 35 mm film the standard and let photographers work handheld.

asteroid_day.label: International Asteroid Day
asteroid_day.intro: A day for the rubble left over from building the solar system, and for the people who keep an eye on the pieces that come close.
funFacts: The date recalls the Tunguska event of 30 June 1908, when an air burst flattened around 2,000 square kilometres of Siberian forest.
The day was initiated in 2014 by a group including Brian May and Stephen Hawking, and the UN adopted it in 2016.
NASA's DART probe struck the moonlet Dimorphos in 2022 and measurably shortened its orbit, the first deflection test.
